checks.claim: Lysenko soaked and chilled winter wheat seed so it could be sown in spring and still bear grain (vernalisation)
checks.note: 'By treating wheat seeds with moisture as well as cold, Lysenko induced them to bear a crop when planted in spring.' Grokipedia: seeds soaked in water at near-freezing temperatures, then sown in spring.

checks.claim: He claimed the change would be inherited
checks.note: Grokipedia: progeny 'retained the modified traits independently of further treatment'; Wikipedia: he 'believed that the vernalized transformation could be inherited'.

checks.claim: Key: only seed of chilled plants, sown unchilled in spring and bearing grain, would test inheritance; the other three describe the treated seed itself or the untreated control
Context: the chilled state is wiped clean as each new embryo forms, so each generation needs its own winter
checks.note: 'The removal of silent chromatin marks at FLC during embryogenesis prevents the inheritance of the vernalized state.' A minority (Li and Liu) argue for epigenetic inheritance; the mainstream view stated is right.

checks.claim: Context: Vavilov at first encouraged Lysenko's work and stopped when it failed to deliver
checks.note: 'It was Vavilov who initially supported Lysenko and encouraged him in his work'; he dropped it when it did not give the expected results.

checks.claim: Lysenko denied genes existed and rejected Mendel's laws
checks.note: 'Lysenko did not believe in genes and only spoke about them to say that they did not exist.'

checks.claim: N. I. Ermolaeva, 'one of his followers', repeated Mendel's pea crosses and reported in 1939 that hybrids did not give 3:1
checks.note: Stark and Seneta 2011: she published in 1939 in Yarovizatsiia (Lysenko's journal) that Mendel's 3:1 principle was false, and Lysenko supported her; Grokipedia calls the data 'Lysenko's own students''. 'Follower' is fair; 'whose work Lysenko backed' is safest.

checks.claim: Kolmogorov re-examined her counts in 1940; key: they strayed from 3:1 only as far as chance allows
checks.note: Kolmogorov 1940, 'On a new confirmation of Mendel's laws': 'a new brilliant confirmation of Mendel's laws'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices (closer to 1:1; blending; acquired traits) are not what he found
Context: Lysenko held that Kolmogorov was wrong
checks.note: Lysenko's 1940 reply 'In response to an article by A.N. Kolmogoroff' concluded Kolmogorov was wrong.

checks.claim: Context quote: he dismissed statistical treatment of data as 'bourgeois formalism'
checks.note: The phrase appears only in Grokipedia's own narrative ('which he dismissed as bourgeois formalism'), not as Lysenko's documented words; Grokipedia's Lysenkoism page, Wikipedia and Stark and Seneta do not have it, and no primary source was found. Quotation marks make it his words. Fix: drop the quotation marks and the label, e.g. 'Lysenko held that Kolmogorov was wrong, and claimed that mathematics had no place in biology' (Wikipedia, unquoted).

checks.claim: Context: two researchers rechecking in 2011 (Stark and Seneta) found flaws in Kolmogorov's method, yet a corrected test still confirmed his conclusion
checks.note: Their chi-squared on families of 20 or more gave p = 0.09 and 0.11: no strong evidence against Mendel, though weaker than Kolmogorov presented.

checks.claim: Stalin approved the VASKhNIL session (Lenin All-Union Academy of Agricultural Sciences), Moscow, August 1948
checks.note: Ran 31 July to 7 August 1948, 'organized by Lysenko and approved by Stalin'; Stalin edited Lysenko's report (Grokipedia; Wikipedia, August 1948 Session).

checks.claim: On the last day Lysenko said the Central Committee had examined his report and approved it
checks.note: 7 August: 'The Central Committee of the Communist Party has examined my report and approved it.'

checks.claim: Key: genetics barred from teaching and research
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'banning its teaching and research in Soviet institutions'; Borinskaya et al. 2019 (Genetics): genetics proclaimed 'an idealistic pseudobiology', curricula purged.

checks.claim: Wrong choices (taught as a rival; kept for animals; put to a field test) did not happen
Context: genetics branded a 'bourgeois pseudoscience'
checks.note: Scare-quoted label, not ascribed to one speaker; Wikipedia describes Lysenko's attack on 'bourgeois pseudoscience' as aimed at genetics. Borinskaya's wording from 1948 is 'idealistic pseudobiology'.

checks.claim: Context: more than 3,000 biologists dismissed or jailed
checks.note: Wikipedia: 'Over 3,000 biologists were fired, and numerous scientists were imprisoned, or executed' (for the campaign as a whole); Grokipedia: over 3,000 ousted after the resolution; Borinskaya 2019: 'several thousands'. Wikipedia's August 1948 Session page gives about 300 'geneticists' persecuted, a narrower count. Survives as stated.

checks.claim: Context: an order went out to destroy fruit-fly stocks
checks.note: 'There was an order to destroy all stocks of Drosophila.' Borinskaya 2019: 'Mutant strains and various genetic preparations were also destroyed', i.e. not only flies.

checks.claim: Context: leaders wanted quick promises after the early-1930s famine, breeding looked slow; ban lifted mid-1960s after he lost his posts
checks.note: Famine of 1932-33 (Wikipedia); 'promised rapid crop yield increases', 'bypassing the need for selective breeding over generations' (Grokipedia); 'The ban was finally lifted in the mid-1960s'; removed as director of the Institute of Genetics in 1965.

checks.claim: 1948 plan (Great Plan for the Transformation of Nature) for forest belts across the steppes; acorns sown in clusters by Lysenko's nest method
checks.note: Grokipedia: clusters of acorns; CIA reading-room translation: acorns sown by 'the Lysenko nest method'.

checks.claim: Lysenko held that plants of one kind do not compete, and crowded seedlings help one another
checks.note: He 'denied that intraspecific competition occurred in nature' (Wikipedia, Lysenkoism); nests 'where members of the same species helped each other'.

checks.claim: Stem: 'The ecologist Vladimir Sukachev followed the plantings in the Ural lands'; context: Sukachev recorded that by September 1951 every nest-planted tree in the Ural lands had died
checks.note: Wikipedia says Sukachev 'recorded' the 100% Ural die-off (no footnote of its own; paragraph cites Brain 2010). Grokipedia credits 'Ural administration reports' with the 100% failure and has Sukachev only as a critic of the method. No primary or historian's text found. Neither source says Sukachev himself followed the Ural plantings. Fix: 'Reports from the Ural lands recorded ...' in the stem, and 'Vladimir Sukachev, an ecologist who opposed Lysenko, ...' as the critic; or keep 'Sukachev recorded' (Wikipedia) and drop 'followed the plantings'.

checks.claim: Key: every tree sown that way (in the Urals) had died by September 1951
checks.note: Both Wikipedia and Grokipedia give 100% in the Urals by September 1951; overall survival elsewhere about 10% (Grokipedia). The key is limited to the Ural plantings by the stem.

checks.claim: Context: crowding seedlings of one kind sharpens competition; a crowded stand survives by self-thinning
checks.note: Stated flatly as the cause of the Ural die-off; the record alone does not single out crowding (steppe drought, nurse crops). The judge's fix ('Sukachev and other ecologists blamed the crowding') is safer.

checks.claim: Vavilov led expeditions to five continents in the 1920s and 1930s
checks.note: About 115 expeditions to 64 countries on five continents, 1916-1933 (Grokipedia; Science History Institute).

checks.claim: Built in Leningrad the world's largest collection of crop seeds
checks.note: 'the world's largest ex situ collection at the time'; Wikipedia 'the world's largest collection of plant seeds'. True of its day; 'of its day' would be exact (the judge's fix).

checks.claim: Key: old local varieties and wild relatives hold genes for traits breeders can cross into crops
checks.note: Domesticated crops 'lacked the genetic diversity to withstand hardships'; crossing with hardier wild kinds; Grokipedia: landraces preserve 'genetic variation resistant to diseases and environmental stresses'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices (cold-trained to grow anywhere; longer storage life; bigger harvests) are not his reason
checks.note: The cold-training lure is Lysenko's idea, false for Vavilov's aim.

checks.claim: Context: wanted since boyhood to end famine
checks.note: 'obsessed from an early age with ending famine'.

checks.claim: Context: arrested by the secret police in 1940 while collecting seeds in Ukraine, for opposing Lysenko
checks.note: NKVD, 6 August 1940, western Ukraine; formal charges were espionage and sabotage, the arrest tied to his opposition to Lysenko.

checks.claim: Context: died of starvation in Saratov prison, 1943
checks.note: 26 January 1943, Saratov, 'starvation and associated complications'; Science History Institute and Borinskaya et al. 2019 say starvation. Wikipedia notes the prison record (pneumonia, dystrophy); dystrophy here means starvation.

checks.claim: Context: through the siege his staff guarded the collection and some starved rather than eat it
checks.note: Counts of the dead conflict (9, at least 19, 28); 'some of them' is safe.

checks.claim: Davenport's Eugenics Record Office, Cold Spring Harbor, New York, from 1910; field workers went door to door; family trees (pedigrees)
Feeblemindedness and pauperism counted as inherited, often through a single gene
checks.note: Grokipedia: the ERO portrayed 'traits such as criminality or pauperism as single-gene recessives'; Morgan objected that Davenport treated feeblemindedness as a unitary Mendelian recessive (Grokipedia, Davenport).

checks.claim: Key: a family tree cannot separate genes from a shared home and upbringing
checks.note: Carr-Saunders: eugenicists could not separate biological heredity from environment.

checks.claim: Wrong choices (mother or father line; skipped generation; sons against daughters) are things a pedigree can show
Context: funded by Mary Harriman and later the Carnegie Institution; Mendelian 'unit characters'
checks.note: Founded 1910 with Mary Harriman's grant; Carnegie took over funding in 1918. 'unit characters' (Grokipedia, Davenport).

checks.claim: Context: Davenport studied the genetics of pellagra, later shown to be a vitamin deficiency
checks.note: 'later shown to be due to a vitamin deficiency' (niacin).

checks.claim: Context: Morgan and Jennings argued he overlooked surroundings and that most human traits depend on many genes
checks.note: Morgan: 'overlooked environmental influences like nutrition and education'; Jennings: most variation from 'multiple interacting genes modulated by environmental factors'. Joint attribution is fair.

checks.claim: Context: 'feebleminded' a loose label; intelligence polygenic, many genes of small effect, plus upbringing
Laughlin, superintendent of the ERO, gave a sworn written deposition in Carrie Buck's case, 1924
checks.note: Superintendent 1910-1939; written testimony 'presented during the trial in his absence' (Wikipedia, Buck v. Bell).

checks.claim: Carrie Buck held at the state colony for the 'feebleminded' (Virginia State Colony for Epileptics and Feeble-Minded)
Quote: 'the shiftless, ignorant, and worthless class of anti-social whites of the South'
checks.note: Matches word for word.

checks.claim: Key: his statement rested on what the colony's doctors told him (he never met her)
checks.note: Lombardo: 'Laughlin parroted language provided to him by the doctors in the case'; Wikipedia: Laughlin 'had never met Buck'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices (own tests at the colony; school record; talks with neighbours) are false
Context: a teacher wrote she was 'very good' in 'deportment and lessons'; taken out of school in sixth grade for housework
checks.note: The two quoted fragments match.

checks.claim: Context: Indiana first sterilisation law 1907; Virginia's 1924 law, which the colony meant this case to test, followed Laughlin's model law
checks.note: 18 states, Virginia in 1924, based laws on his model; Priddy tabled every other order to test the law on Buck (Encyclopedia Virginia).

checks.claim: Quote: a social worker said the baby had 'a look about it that is not quite normal'
checks.note: Matches word for word.

checks.claim: Stem: 'Arthur Estabrook ... held a coin before the baby's eyes and judged her feebleminded'
checks.note: Estabrook testified he gave her 'the usual test for a baby of about six months old' and she failed (DNALC). The coin comes from his photograph: DNALC says the test 'this picture seems to suggest, was to hold a coin'; Lombardo (DNALC clip summary) says Estabrook 'apparently' used a coin; the Library of Virginia says 'Mrs. Dobbs [the foster mother] waved a coin in front of Vivian's face'. Who held it is not settled. Fix: 'Arthur Estabrook of the Eugenics Record Office said that she had failed the usual test for a baby her age, which seems to have been a coin waved before her eyes, and judged her feebleminded.'

checks.claim: Supreme Court upheld the sterilisation in 1927 (8-1, 2 May), counting Vivian as a third generation
Key: on the honour roll in first grade
checks.note: Lombardo: 'Vivian was on the honor roll in the first grade at Venable School'; Wikipedia: April 1931.

checks.claim: Wrong choices (grade skipped; IQ in lowest tenth; special class) have no record behind them
Context quote: Gould, 'a perfectly normal, quite average student'
checks.note: Matches.

checks.claim: Context: died of an infection at eight in 1932
checks.note: Enteric colitis after measles; exact date conflicts across sources, none given.

checks.claim: Context: 'a coin held before a baby of about seven months'
checks.note: Age 'about seven months' is right (DNALC). The coin is hedged in every source (see above); 'a coin apparently waved before a baby of about seven months' is safe.

checks.claim: Context: Holmes, 'Three generations of imbeciles are enough.'; California about 20,000 sterilised; never expressly overturned
checks.note: California '20,000 of the 60,000' (1909-1960); Buck v. Bell 'has never expressly overturned'.

checks.claim: Twenty doctors and three officials tried at Nuremberg for experiments on prisoners of war and civilians
checks.note: 20 physicians and 3 SS officials (Brack, Rudolf Brandt, Sievers).

checks.claim: Three American judges; ten principles set out in the verdict of August 1947
checks.note: Beals, Sebring, Crawford (plus an alternate); verdict 20 August 1947, ten points under 'Permissible Medical Experiments'.

checks.claim: Key and quote: 'The voluntary consent of the human subject is absolutely essential.'
checks.note: Word for word; it is the first principle's first, single sentence.

checks.claim: Context quotes: 'force, fraud, deceit, duress'; 'an understanding and enlightened decision'; duty on each individual who initiates, directs or engages in the experiment
Wrong choices are the Code's 3rd (animal tests), 2nd (unprocurable by other means) and 6th (risk not exceeding the problem's humanitarian importance) principles
Context: accused argued no law distinguished lawful from unlawful experiments; Code never made law; later codes modelled on it
checks.note: 'there was no law that differentiated between legal and illegal experiments'; 'has not been officially accepted as law by any nation'; 'prototype for all future codes'.

checks.claim: Fifth principle bars experiments where there is an a priori reason to believe death or disabling injury will occur
Key and quote: 'except, perhaps, in those experiments where the experimental physicians also serve as subjects'
checks.note: Word for word.

checks.claim: Wrong choices (condemned prisoners; deadly disease; paid subjects): the Code makes no such exceptions
Context: ninth principle, a subject free to bring an experiment to an end; tenth, the scientist in charge ready to stop it
checks.note: Ninth: 'During the course of the experiment the human subject should be at liberty to bring the experiment to an end' if he has reached the state where continuing 'seems to him to be impossible'. The card drops the condition; fine as a summary. The judge's suggested ninth-principle question is accurate if its key is 'He is free to bring the experiment to an end' and the stem carries the condition; its three lures (must finish; only with the doctor's leave; only if a judge agrees) are all false under the text.

unit_notes: All ten checked on the web. Seven ok, one error, two uncertain. ERROR Q2 (5ebb718ad9): 'bourgeois formalism' is quoted as Lysenko's words but appears only in Grokipedia's own narrative; drop the quotation marks or use Wikipedia's 'claimed that mathematics had no place in biology' unquoted. UNCERTAIN Q4 (af30276e93): the 100% Ural die-off by September 1951 is in Wikipedia and Grokipedia, but Wikipedia credits Sukachev's record and Grokipedia 'Ural administration reports'; no source says Sukachev 'followed the plantings'. UNCERTAIN Q8 (e7f51fb990): every source hedges the coin test ('seems to suggest', 'apparently'), and the Library of Virginia says the foster mother, Mrs. Dobbs, waved the coin, not Estabrook. Quotations checked word for word: the Nuremberg Code (Avalon), Laughlin's deposition phrase, the social worker's remark, Gould, Holmes, and Lysenko's Central Committee line. Kolmogorov 1940: 'a new brilliant confirmation of Mendel's laws'; Stark and Seneta 2011 confirm his conclusion with a corrected test. For the judge's proposed fruit-fly rewrite of Q3: Wikipedia records 'an order to destroy all stocks of Drosophila', but Borinskaya et al. 2019 (Genetics) say 'Mutant strains and various genetic preparations were also destroyed', so a 'Lab mice' or 'Maize plants' lure may not be cleanly false. The 3,000 figure varies with the source (about 300 geneticists on Wikipedia's session page; 'several thousands' in Borinskaya).
